title: The Undertow of the coast road
premise: Jonah Ishikawa, a bridge inspector who measures everything—including his failing marriage—in millimeters of movement, learns that the coastal house where his late mother once took in foster children is scheduled for auction and demolition to make way for a seawall. Returning to the coast road, he uncovers letters, debts, and a half-brother he never knew existed, forcing him to choose between preserving his inheritance of silence or breaking it. As the auction date collides with the anniversary of his mother's death, Jonah must decide whether to bid on a house or on the truth. The novel ends not with the house saved but with Jonah speaking his goodbye aloud at the demolition—reconciled, if not restored, and finally an owner of his own life.
about_author: Petra Eriksen is a former structural engineer who spent a decade inspecting bridges along the Pacific coast before turning to fiction full-time. Her work examines how people inherit places, silences, and obligations—and what it costs to put any of them down.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Jonah inspects a deteriorating bridge, narrating his marriage through engineering metaphors while his wife Dana sleeps facing away. A letter arrives: the Ishikawa house on the coast road enters auction next month. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: numb routine cracked open by an unwelcome summons.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Jonah catalogs his life like an asset register—job, mortgage, a marriage measured in polite intervals—and realizes he owns none of it emotionally. He tells Dana about the auction; she hears an escape plan he hasn't admitted to himself. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: quiet self-indictment.

chapters.title: Coast Road, Northbound
chapters.summary: Jonah drives up alone, the sea appearing and disappearing between headlands. The house stands boarded, tagged for demolition after auction. A neighbor, Ruth Calloway, recognizes him and says something that unsettles him: 'Your mother kept more than children here.' POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: dread braided with homesickness.

chapters.title: What the House Kept
chapters.summary: Inside the sealed house, Jonah finds his childhood intact under dust—height marks on a doorframe, his mother's ledgers. One ledger lists payments from a name he doesn't recognize: T. Ishikawa. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: the past turning physical and accusatory.

chapters.title: Dana's Side of the Span
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter in Dana's POV: five years of Jonah's absences, her own abandoned career, the miscarriage they never discussed. She interprets his trip as abandonment beginning again. POV: Dana. Emotional beat: grief reframed as anger.

chapters.title: T. Ishikawa
chapters.summary: Ruth reveals that Theo Ishikawa—Jonah's father's son by a first marriage—lived in the house until recently, paying his stepmother's medical bills in secret. Jonah never knew he existed. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: the ground shifting under an assumed history.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Back home, Jonah researches probate records and finds his mother refinanced the house twice to fund foster placements, leaving debt only Theo tried to cover. He drafts an email to Theo and deletes it four times. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: cowardice examined at close range.

chapters.title: Bidding War
chapters.summary: A developer, Marren Coastal Group, announces plans for the seawall project; locals split between jobs and memory. Ruth organizes a token community bid. Jonah realizes whoever wins buys the demolition too. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: stakes widening beyond family.

chapters.title: Letters in the Wall Cavity
chapters.summary: Inspecting the foundation—habit, not sentiment—Jonah finds a tin in a wall cavity: unsent letters from his mother to Theo, written over thirty years, asking forgiveness she never mailed. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: inherited shame made legible.

chapters.title: Theo
chapters.summary: Jonah tracks Theo to a boatyard two towns south. Their first meeting is wary, transactional—until Theo says, 'She asked you to say goodbye too, didn't she? That's why you came.' POV: Theo. Emotional beat: recognition across a lifetime of absence.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Theo recounts being sent away at fourteen when the second marriage began, surviving on work and resentment, returning only to pay bills anonymously. He refuses the sentimental bid: 'Houses don't forgive people.' POV: Theo. Emotional beat: hardened grief resisting consolation.

chapters.title: Joint Failure
chapters.summary: Jonah returns home mid-crisis: Dana has taken a job offer in another city. Their confrontation strips the marriage to its load-bearing members—he has been present like a beam, not a partner. POV: alternating Jonah/Dana. Emotional beat: honest rupture before possible repair.

chapters.title: Inspection Report
chapters.summary: Jonah writes Dana a letter modeled on his inspection reports, itemizing the defects he brought to the marriage and the repairs he never attempted. It is the most honest document of his life. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: confession as craft.

chapters.title: Community Hearing
chapters.summary: At the county hearing, testimony splits the town; Theo speaks publicly for the first time, revealing his identity and his mother's foster legacy. The room's judgment turns toward preservation—but money leans toward Marren. POV: Theo. Emotional beat: public exposure as liberation.

chapters.title: The Bid
chapters.summary: Pooling nothing, Jonah and Theo decide to bid anyway—not to win, but to force the house's story into the record before it falls. Dana, reading Jonah's letter, drives up unannounced. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: reckless hope.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: The auction proceeds under gray skies. Jonah and Theo are outbid early by Marren; Ruth's coalition folds. But the auctioneer pauses—the county has flagged the parcel pending a heritage review. A stay, not a salvation. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: defeat edged with reprieve.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: The heritage review fails; demolition is set for three weeks out. Theo wants to walk away; Jonah insists on one thing: they go through the house together, room by room, before the machines come. POV: Theo. Emotional beat: reluctant return.

chapters.title: Room by Room
chapters.summary: Brothers move through the house—Theo's old room, the kitchen where their mother fed other people's children, the doorframe with both boys' height marks side by side, decades apart. They read the unsent letters aloud. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: shared mourning replacing parallel solitude.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: On the last morning, neighbors gather on the coast road. Before the excavators start, Jonah takes the microphone no one offered and says the goodbye his mother never sent and he never spoke—to her, to Theo, to the child he and Dana lost. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: climax; speech as survival.

chapters.title: The Falling
chapters.summary: The house comes down in eleven minutes. Theo puts his hand on Jonah's shoulder—their first touch as brothers. Ruth collects a doorframe plank for the town hall. POV: Theo. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into witness.

chapters.title: Load Path
chapters.summary: Weeks later: Jonah transfers inland, takes a job teaching inspection to young engineers, and begins counseling. Dana visits; nothing is promised, but they sit on a bench over the new seawall and talk without measuring. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: repair begun, not completed.

chapters.title: Owner
chapters.summary: Final chapter: Jonah stands on the empty lot where the house stood, the sea beyond, and signs his name in the visitor book Ruth keeps at the memorial cairn. For the first time, he writes 'owner' under occupation—of his grief, his choices, his voice. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: resolution; tenancy ends, ownership begins.
